shortSummary: Sini Tistelgrén describes an AI factory as a delivery system built on intent, architecture, security, independent verification, ownership and operational feedback. She explains why a quick prototype still needs a production path, and proposes bounded loops with executable controls and evidence.
longSummary: Sini Tistelgrén argues that generating code quickly does not remove the work of taking a change safely into production. Her AI factory connects six stations—intent, design, build, verify, release and operate—through shared foundations and explicitly owned checks. In enterprises, much of the difficulty lies in making existing architecture, data ownership, business rules and decision reasons accessible to agents. She describes assessment findings in which unclear requirements, competing rules, weak testing, ambiguous release ownership and missing production feedback push risk downstream. A delivery-address example illustrates how acceptance criteria, architectural rules, independent verification, controlled release and rollback could work together. Routine changes may use pre-approved policies while people remain responsible for intent, controls and exceptions. She recommends starting with one loosely coupled value stream, measuring its baseline and reinvesting capacity in the surrounding delivery system.

takeaways.point: A working prototype expresses intent but still needs the architecture, access, release, operations and support work required for production.
An AI factory should connect intent, design, build, verification, release and operation through shared fundamentals.
Agents need written domain rules, tested interfaces, decision reasons and bounded access to the architecture the organisation actually has.
Control ownership and independent verification matter; the author of a change should not be its sole approver.
Start with one bounded value stream and a baseline, then measure lead time, failed changes and the cost of accepted delivery rather than output volume alone.
